abstract_text: The distribution of basking sharks (Cetorhinus maximus) around the Isle of Arran in the Clyde sea area on the west coast of Scotland, UK was investigated during July 1997. A network of shore based volunteers conducted visual searches between 06:00 and 22:00 from seven vantage points for a total of 1538 hours over 20 days between July 6 and 28. Twenty-nine sightings were recorded. A plankton sampling programme was carried out in the same area and over the same time period. The majority of shark sightings occurred in the afternoon and evening corresponding to an increase in zooplankton abundance during this period. Three peaks in shark sightings occurred over the study period which followed peaks in zooplankton abundance with a lag of one to three days. The spatial distribution of shark sightings was also associated with the distribution of zooplankton in the area. Increases in the number of sharks occurred when zooplankton dry weights were at the maximum normally found in the area. This study has shown, therefore, that fine-scale spatio-temporal variability in the distribution of basking sharks can be explained in terms of patchiness in the distribution and abundance of zooplankton.

title: Length-at-birth of the sandbar shark, Carcharhinus plumbeus, in Delaware Bay

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, University of Rhode Island, Kingston, RI 02881, USA
National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, National Marine Fisheries Service, Northeast Fisheries Science Center, 28 Tarzwell Dr., Narragansett, RI 02882-1199, USA

abstract_text: Young-of-the-year sandbar sharks grow in length before their umbilical scars are healed. This study takes that into account by separating umbilical scar healing stages and produces a more accurate length-at-birth than studies which report the lengths of sandbar sharks with open umbilical scars. We examined 798 sandbar sharks captured by gill net or longline in Delaware Bay between 1995 and 1997. Six distinct umbilical scar healing stages were termed cord-remains, open-fresh, partly-healed, mostly-healed, well-healed and none. Sharks with the three earliest umbilical healing stages did not differ in length, thus represented the length-at-birth. The mean length-at-birth is 49.3 cm ±0.3 cm fork length (95% confidence interval, n=238) with a range of 40 to 55 cm fork length in Delaware Bay. Our results are comparable to published reports of sandbar length-at-birth along the US east coast and therefore do not support the hypothesis that sandbar sharks are born 'somewhat' smaller in the northern pupping range.

title: History and management of the dogfish fishery of British Columbia, Canada

authors.affiliation: Fisheries Centre, UBC, 2204 Main Mall, Vancouver, BC V6T 1Z4

abstract_text: The fishery for dogfish (Squalus acanthias) of British Columbia is one of the oldest shark fisheries in the world. This paper describes the main features in the long evolution of this fishery. It also analyses the current situation and the management system of the fishery. Presently, this is a small fishery characterized by strong market limitations. Although there is a reasonably modern management system for the fishery, the apparent success to keep the dogfish stocks at healthy levels for the major part of the 125+ years of the fishery is more a product of the lack of strong demand for dogfish which has offered a fortuitous protection to the stock. Some suggestions for improvements to the stock assessment and possible ways to develop the fishery are given.

title: Catch and effort data of whale sharks in the Philippines

authors.affiliation: Kabang Kalikasan ng Pilipinas (WWF-Philippines), No. 32-A Maalindog St., UP Village, Diliman, Quezon City 1101, Philippines

abstract_text: Catch volume and trade of the whale shark fishery for the 1997-1998 season was monitored by WWF-Philippines and Silliman University. Methods of data collection include site-visits to coastal villages involved in whale shark and manta fishery, market surveys, fishers' interviews and daily landing-site enumeration. Eight fishery sites were identified in the 1997 season, the major landing sites of which were in Pamilacan, Bohol and Talisayan, Misamis Oriental. A fishery site in Sorsogon, Luzon is recently operational for the 1998 season. Fishery profiles and changes in activity patterns related to whale shark fishery in these sites are presented. Increasing fishing effort, due to increasing demand, and decreasing catch per unit effort characterized the fishery. Management strategies employing Integrated Conservation and Development projects protecting both whale sharks and the fishing population dependent on them was recommended in the previous year. This recommendation is being evaluated against a government directive on total ban on whale shark fishery and trade.

title: Sharks associated with the gulf menhaden Brevoortia patronus fishery and their relevance to shark populations of the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico

abstract_text: We describe the shark bycatch in the U.S. gulf menhaden fishery; their species composition, fates, distribution and estimate the annual number of sharks caught by the fishery. Ten species of sharks were identified, with blacktip sharks Carcharhinus limbatus accounting for 50% of those observed. Approximately 75% of the sharks encountered died, 12% were released disoriented and 8% were released healthy. Using loglinear and logit models we determined spatial and temporal patterns in the shark bycatch. Contrasts revealed the odds of observing a fishing set with shark bycatch was significantly greater in June-August than September-October. The odds of observing shark bycatch during April-May was also significantly different from September-October. However, these differences were only apparent east of 93 degrees W (central Louisiana). For the 1994 and 1995 fishing seasons we estimated an annual take of approximately 30,000 sharks. Stomach analyses on sharks indicated that the menhaden schools were functioning as a foraging base for those sharks captured. While detailed age and growth information were not collected, comparisons to length distributions in the literature indicated that the fishery appears to be impacting the summer nursery grounds of sharks in the northern Gulf of Mexico.

title: Density effects of oophagous tadpoles of Chirixalus eiffingeri (Anura: Rhacophoridae): Importance of maternal brood care

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, National Changhua University of Education, Taiwan
Department of Biology, National Changhua University of Education, Taiwan
Dept. of Zoology, National Taiwan University, Taiwan
Dept. of Zoology, National Taiwan University, Taiwan

abstract_text: We studied the density-dependent aspects of growth, development, and survivorship of arboreal tadpoles of Chirixalus eiffingeri in bamboo forests at the Experimental Forest of the National Taiwan University at Chitou, Taiwan, from May-September 1995. Newly hatched tadpoles were randomly assigned to one of the three treatments: low (LD), medium (MD), and high density (HD) (six, 18, and 54 tadpoles/bamboo stump, respectively), and each treatment consisted of 15 replicates. Tadpoles are obligatorily oophagous; thus, growth, development, and survivorship of tadpoles are totally dependent upon trophic egg availability. Tadpoles in all treatments increased in mass during development, but LD and MD tadpoles grew faster and weighed significantly heavier than HD tadpoles by week 5. During the first 5 weeks of development, the biomass increase of tadpoles (BMI) in successful nests was substantially greater than zero and was significantly different between treatments, indicating that female frogs are capable of increasing the supply of trophic eggs as the tadpole number increased in MD and HD treatments. Body size at metamorphosis was density-dependent but the time required to reach metamorphosis was not, which was different from earlier studies on pond breeders. This discrepancy is probably due to the different feeding habits (i.e., herbivory versus oophagy) and size-selective feeding behavior. Results suggest that the energetic reserves of female frogs for brooding strongly affect the growth, development, and survivorship of tadpoles.

title: Contributions to the life history of the redback salamander: preliminary evidence for kin recognition

authors.affiliation: Biological Sciences, Towson University, Towson, MD 21252 USA
Biological Sciences, Towson University, Towson, MD 21252 USA

abstract_text: We tested two questions critical to the reproductive life history of the redback salamander (Plethodon cinereus): (1) Do females recognize and preferentially brood their own eggs during pair-wise discrimination trials? (2) Are hatchlings able to recognize their mother using substrate-borne chemical cues, and if so, is this ability innate or learned? To address the first question, we tested brooding females collected from the field within a few days of oviposition. They were given a choice of their own eggs and those of a conspecific female, and their association monitored over a 24 h period. To address the second question we collected 60 females within 24 h post-oviposition, and divided them into two groups. The eggs of group 1 were raised by their mothers until they hatched. The eggs of group 2 were isolated on filter paper throughout development. Beginning at 2 weeks post-hatching, each juvenile was tested twice (24 h each) in pair-wise trials contrasting unmarked filter paper with filter paper scented with maternal odors. Our results confirm maternal egg recognition in P. cinereus, and we present preliminary data suggesting that juveniles chemically imprint on their mother during the prolonged maternal brooding period.

title: Reproductive success in the bullfrog, Rana catesbeiana

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Ontario, N1G 2W1
Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Ontario, N1G 2W1

abstract_text: We studied mating behavior and reproductive success in a wild, northern population of bullfrogs (Rana catesbeiana). The predominant selective mechanism in this system was female choice. Male bullfrogs gathered annually at traditional chorusing sites where they competed aggressively or employed alternate mating strategies in an attempt to acquire mates. Females entered the choruses briefly to select a mate, engage in amplexus, and deposit eggs. Compared with males that were unsuccessful in obtaining mates, reproductively successful males were larger, had longer tenures in the choruses, spent more of their tenure calling, and had previous chorusing experience. Male size was related to reproductive effort with larger males losing proportionately more weight over the chorusing season. In females, clutch volume was positively related to body size with large females depositing egg masses up to three times larger than those of small females. There was no evidence of assortative mating by body size. We also postulated that, because of a low population density, this system may best be described as a lek in contrast to the resource-defense system described previously for this species.

title: Maternal care and tadpole survival in Dendrobates pumilio: Are food and shelter really enough?

authors.affiliation: School of Biological Sciences, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY 40506 USA

abstract_text: I conducted field studies to determine the influence of female Dendrobates pumilio on offspring survival through two forms of maternal care; rearing site selection and nutritional provisioning. Female D. pumilio transport tadpoles from hatching sites to water-filled leaf axils where they are tended until metamorphosis. I assessed availability and variability of rearing axils (pH, temperature, water volume, height, cover), female choice of rearing sites, and effects of site characters on tadpole survival. Rearing sites are abundant and highly variable. While female choice is best predicted by a combination of low height and pH, tadpole survival is best predicted by variance in axil temperature. These results suggest that although females deposit their tadpoles non-randomly, rearing site selection does not influence tadpole fitness. Females return to tadpole rearing sites to provide eggs for their tadpoles to eat throughout development. I observed females tending tadpoles to determine the influence of provisioning on tadpole fitness. Provisioning behaviors such as time to first feeding, frequency of feedings, and number of eggs per feeding are highly variable. Although there is substantial variation in provisioning, preliminary analyses indicate that predation [text partly illegible] provisioning on tadpole survival, limiting the potential for further evolution of provisioning.

title: Reproductive trade-offs in the red-backed salamander, Plethodon cinereus: The effects of parental care

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, Binghamton University (SUNY), Binghamton, New York, 13902-6000 USA
Department of Biological Sciences, Binghamton University (SUNY), Binghamton, New York, 13902-6000 USA

abstract_text: Iteroparous animals that have substantial investment in parental care should invest energy differentially into growth and reproduction according to size and age. Smaller, younger animals should invest more energy in growth for future reproductive benefits, while larger, older animals should invest more energy in reproduction and parental care. In this study, 22 gravid female red-backed salamanders (Plethodon cinereus) were induced to oviposit in the laboratory, and brooding behavior was recorded for salamanders with body sizes ranging from 34 mm to 53 mm SVL. Female body size was positively correlated with clutch size. Females that oviposited atypically and/or terminated parental care by oophagy were significantly smaller than females who reared their clutches normally. These results suggest that smaller females may forego reproduction to invest in growth, while larger females should always invest in reproduction.

title: Female preferences for multiple male traits in the advertisement calls of the neotropical hylid Smilisca phaeota

authors.affiliation: Dept. of Zoology, University of Texas, Austin, TX 78712, USA

abstract_text: Males of the hylid Smilisca phaeota have complex advertisement calls which show a large amount of variation in several frequency related traits. Two of these traits were found to be negatively correlated with each other in the natural population studied. Female preferences for male calls were tested in and around the correlation of these two traits. Initial results demonstrated that females have directional preferences for both traits when measured independently. Females were found to have preferences which exert a stabilizing effect on the correlation in the two trait space. As a result of these preferences, the directionality of preference for any one trait taken independently can change depending on the relation of that trait to a second trait.

title: Biparental care in a neotropical bromeliad-breeding tree frog, Osteocephalus planiceps

authors.affiliation: University of Oklahoma, Department of Zoology, Norman, Oklahoma 73019 USA

abstract_text: The reproductive behaviors of a bromeliad-breeding tree frog, Osteocephalus planiceps (Hylidae) were studied in Amazonian Peru. Pairs of this species form where males defend oviposition territories (i.e. bromeliads), and females return periodically to amplex with the males to lay fertilized trophic eggs for their developing tadpoles. To determine the extent of biparental care and how biparental care and resource defense affect the mating system, I relocated bromeliads within a 1-ha study area into clumped versus isolated oviposition sites. In addition, 12 artificial bromeliads were provided so that egg deposition and tadpole survival could be monitored at those sites. All matings in the study site were recorded for a five-month period, and the number of metamorphs produced in the artificial bromeliads was used to evaluate individual reproductive success. Although males and females form monogamous pairs due to site-fidelity, several ecological factors seem to maintain a rather fluid mating system. Limited oviposition sites, relative proximity of oviposition sites (one male's territory may include more than one oviposition site and, therefore, can potentially accommodate more than one female), and high predation pressure all contribute to continuous changes in the mating system.

title: Diversifying selection due to female preferences and males that respond appropriately in the neotropical hylid Smilisca phaeota

authors.affiliation: Dept. of Zoology, University of Texas, Austin, TX 78712, USA

abstract_text: Females of the hylid Smilisca phaeota were found to have significantly different preferences for male advertisment calls under different simulated chorusing behaviors. Male Smilisca phaeota often try to overlap their calls with those of another male. This behavior is common but not ubiquitous. Females presented with a pair of test calls given in an overlapping sequence that was controlled for lead calling. Females preference was found to be significant and opposite that of females given the same pair of test calls in an alternating sequence. Male chorusing behavior was found to reflect the apparent diversifying selection from female preferences. Male-male interactions were recorded in the field using males of noticably different call types. Males which had a lower dominant frequency correspond to the male type chosen by females when test calls were given alternately. Males with a higher dominant frequency correspond with the test calls that were chosen by females in the overlapping test. Interactions of male-male pairs in the field have shown that males behave in a way that would be expected by the female choice.

title: Mating system of the green anaconda (Eunectes murinus) in the Venezuelan Llanos

authors.affiliation: University of Tennessee, Dept. of EEB, Knoxville TN 37996-0900

abstract_text: Sexual selection and mating system theories predict that individuals will be more selective the higher the mating investment they make. Hence, animals that do not make a high reproductive investment will increase their fitness by increasing number of matings, while animals that have a high investment per mating will be "choosy". While studying the mating system of the anaconda, we opportunistically collected 45 breeding aggregations for six years. Females lie apparently passive in shallow water while the males coil around her (males number from 1 to 17, with a mean of 3.8). No fights or ritualized displays were seen among the males. Each female is attractive to males for about four weeks throughout the breeding season, which lasts from mid-February to mid-May. Longer males were found with heavier females (r= 0.48; p= 0.008) and the latter were courted by a greater number of males (r= 0.44; p= 0.02). This suggests that males prefer to court females with higher fecundity and breeding status, since random mating would not produce this tendencies. Due to the short time that the breeding season lasts (in respect to the duration of the breeding ball), and the fact that receptive females are not clumped together, it is unlikely that one male can find many females in one season. Although a lot remains to be studied, it appears that the mating system of the anacondas is polyandric; where males select the more fecund females.

title: Diet and reproduction of the Common Death Adder (Acanthophis antarcticus) from Papua New Guinea: Lack of ecological convergence with vipers?

authors.affiliation: Dept. of Herpetology, California Academy of Sciences, Golden Gate Park, San Francisco, CA 94110-4599

abstract_text: Common death adders (Elapidae) from Australia have convergent reproductive and dietary adaptations with vipers. They reproduce biannually, show ontogenetic shifts from endothermic to ectothermic prey, and are ambush predators. I examined 208 Acanthophis antarcticus from the collections of the California Academy of Sciences. Morphometric data, sex, age, seasonal reproductive status, size of eggs or follicles, and stomach and hindgut contents were determined. Preliminary results suggest that approximately 30% of snakes had hindgut or stomach contents. Some examples of hindgut and stomach contents included lizard eggs, insect legs, a skink jaw, unidentified bone fragments, and possibly fur. Therefore these death adders appear to prey mostly on ectotherms. Sizes of adult Australian Acanthophis antarcticus from previous studies were on average 30% larger than the Papua New Guinea specimens examined. Initial results show that the majority of females from Papua New Guinea were gravid in December, implying annual reproductivity. Thus these smaller snakes are not displaying convergent ecological characteristics with vipers like their Australian counterparts.

title: Ecomorphological evolution of the feeding biology of crotaphytid lizards

authors.affiliation: Department of Integrative Biology and Museum of Vertebrate Zoology, 3060 VLSB, University of California, Berkeley, CA 94720-3140 USA

abstract_text: Crotaphytid lizards exhibit a morphological trend in several musculo-skeletal characteristics of the trophic apparatus that are correlated with ecological and behavioral attributes, particularly concerning saurophagy and durophagy. Quantification of bite-force performance of taxa representing the primary crotaphytid morphotypes, with respect to trophic apparatus structure, provides performance parameters that relate trophic apparatus structure to dietary ecology and feeding behavior. Data on trophic apparatus musculo-skeletal structure, bite-force performance, feeding behavior, and dietary ecology permit the generation of testable predictions of ecomorphological relationships for other crotaphytid taxa. Examination of crotaphytid feeding biology within a comparative phylogenetic framework reveals that crotaphytids exhibit concordant evolution among trophic apparatus morphology and performance, dietary ecology, and feeding behavior. In addition, increased saurophagy, together with correlated specializations at several levels, appears to have evolved convergently within the Crotaphytidae.

title: Prediction and interpretation of the abundance of alligators in lentic environments

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, USA 32611; US Geological Survey - Biological Resources Division, Gainesville, Florida, USA 32653

abstract_text: Previous analyses indicated that American alligator (Alligator mississippiensis) population densities in 60 Florida lakes were significantly correlated with parameters historically used to evaluate system trophic state (total phosphorus, total nitrogen, water column chlorophyll a, and water transparency). Recent examination of these and other data have begun to reveal some interesting patterns regarding environmental factors and the abundance of this crocodilian. Alligator density was uncorrelated with limnetic zone fish biomass and only slightly correlated with littoral zone fish biomass, but was strongly correlated with whole-lake fish biomass (r2 = 0.45, p < 0.0001). Other environmental factors which were found to covary with alligator population size were lake color (r2 = 0.37, p < 0.0001) and macrophyte coverage (r2 = 0.28, p = 0.0015); those which were inversely related were mean lake depth (r2 = 0.49, p < 0.0001) and percentage of human-developed shoreline (r2 = 0.38, p < 0.0001). Finally, while as much as 55% of the variation in alligator population densities among lakes could be accounted for by total phosphorus (p < 0.0001), multiple linear regressions using other parameters (plant coverage, water transparency, and fish biomass) could account for up to 78% of the variation in abundance (p < 0.0001). These models are discussed with respect to ecological processes present in lakes and their usefulness to game managers and to scientists who attempt to detect human impacts on populations.

title: Environmental variation and socioecology

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, Binghamton, NY 13902-6000 USA

abstract_text: Animal dispersion patterns are influenced by the distribution and abundance of resources and other individuals, both of which are features of the local environment. A previous study indicates that moisture determines the extent to which food and mates are limited for red-backed salamanders (Plethodon cinereus), so predictable differences in moisture levels between populations may result in different dispersion patterns. I monitored shelter use and cohabitation at two sites (wetter vs. drier) using mark-recapture to determine whether shelter fidelity and incidence of cohabitation differ between sites. Both males and females at the wetter site demonstrated lower fidelity, but only females at the wetter site exhibited greater incidence of intrasexual cohabitation. Wetter site males showed low occurrences of intrasexual cohabitation, as did drier site males and females. These results indicate that salamanders in wetter habitats may not hold fixed territories, probably in response to increased food availability. Low fidelity and low intrasexual cohabitation by wetter site males may indicate the existence of ephemeral mating territories. Differences in spacing patterns in response to local environmental conditions may have important repercussions for salamander population dynamics and sexual selection.

title: Spatial and temporal components of fishes in Ohio River embayments

authors.affiliation: Ohio Cooperative Fish & Wildlife Research Unit, B & Z Bldg., 1735 Columbus Ohio USA 43210

abstract_text: The United States has approximately 55 x 10^5 km of rivers. From this total only 1.9% are considered worthy of Federal protection (< 100,000 km), due primarily to human induced changes on the landscape. The Ohio River exhibits anthropogenic scars, as do the embayments associated with the river. Between Parkersburg, WV and Cincinnati, OH I sampled six embayments with different geomorphology, upstream landuse, and habitat conditions. Fishes were collected from these habitats using both gill nets and electrofishing equipment from April through October 1997. I examined habitat use patterns over different spatial scales and found variable patterns in both micro- and macro-scale habitat use. For example, sunfish (Lepomis sp.) used near shore areas in all embayments. Gizzard shad (Dorosoma cepedianum) were collected everywhere in shallow embayments and only in open water areas in deep embayments. On a landscape level fish densities changed as a result of up- mid- or downstream location within an embayment. Integrating information on landuse, physical characteristics, and fish assemblages over different spatial and temporal scales will result in a more complete understanding of the factors influencing these patterns. This information has the potential to inspire better conservation and restoration efforts for these unique habitats along the Ohio River.

title: The effect of body morphology and habitat structural complexity on predator inspection behavior in coral reef fishes

authors.affiliation: School of Natural Resources & Environment, University of Michigan, 430 East University Ave., Ann Arbor, MI 48109-1115 USA

abstract_text: Predator inspection behavior was investigated in three sympatric species of coral reef fish that differed in body morphology, and in two habitats that differed in structural complexity. It was hypothesized that the deep-bodied species would exhibit the riskiest behavior during predator inspections due to their protection from gape-limited predators, and that the shallow-bodied species would be risk-averse. It was also expected that the riskiest inspection behavior would occur in the most complex habitat, due to the presence of prey refuges. Bluehead wrasse, the species most at risk due to the slender body morphology, inspected the predator at greater distances than the other species (ocean surgeonfish, foureye butterflyfish). The percentage of inspections tended to increase with increased body depth across species, indicating risk-averse behavior by the wrasse. Inspection distances decreased in complex habitats for wrasse and surgeonfish, but not butterflyfish, the species with the greatest body depth. Similarly, the percentage of inspections tended to increase in the complex habitat for wrasse and surgeonfish, but not butterflyfish. These data suggest that individuals assessed their overall predation risk related to body morphology and adjusted their inspection behavior, whereas habitat complexity differences played a minor role in predator inspection behavior.

title: Spatial isolation in drainage lakes: implications for community ecology of fishes

authors.affiliation: Dept. of Zoology, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON M5S 3G5

abstract_text: Although lakes are often inter-connected waterbodies, few studies have examined isolation among lakes as a determinant of fish species diversity and/or community composition. In this study I examine the fish species composition and spatial arrangement of 52 lakes located within two south-central Ontario watersheds, and assess the degree of spatial isolation between lakes. Measures of lake isolation incorporated watercourse distance, lake elevation, upstream watercourse distance, and waterbodies as fish "stepping stones". Many of these isolation measures were based on ecological considerations, i.e. the "challenges" a fish faces in moving between lakes, as compared to the straight-line distance between sampling locations which is often used in studies of this nature. Eight isolation measures were examined for their degree of association with patterns in fish species composition. The results indicated that conventional straight-line distance between lakes does not accurately portray the degree of isolation. This study illustrates the importance of examining alternative measures of lake isolation when exploring patterns in fish species distributions, since the isolation of waterbodies increase the rate of local extinction. Therefore, interconnected lakes could potentially provide a "rescue effect" for lakes with threatened aquatic fauna.

title: Mechanisms influencing sizes and survival of age-0 fathead minnows (Pimephales promelas) in two different nutrient regimes

authors.affiliation: University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, T6G 2E9

abstract_text: Factors that affect growth rate (e.g. food supply) should affect juvenile survival and thus year-class strength since the principle sources of mortality for young fish-predation and starvation-are size dependent. In 1996, experimental ponds (area=360 m2/pond) were used to study the effects of nutrient addition on production, growth and survival of age-0 fathead minnows. Each pond was divided in half; one side was treated regularly with inorganic fertilizers (P, N) to maintain nutrient concentrations at levels three times higher than control sides. Chl a was measured to be 7 fold greater in treated versus untreated pond sides. Number of eggs hatched and end-of-season age-0 fish survival and sizes were also greater in the treated pond sides. We analyzed otolith microstructure to investigate the mechanisms behind the observed contrasts in age-0 lengths and survival in the different nutrient regimes. Hatching distributions and back-calculated age-0 fish lengths were compared with those observed throughout the season. Surprisingly, preliminary results suggest age-0 fish survival was not directly influenced by size-selective mortality. Instead, treatment survivors hatched over the entire spawning season; control survivors hatched primarily in the second half of the spawning season. These results suggest that conditions during early periods of growth can influence lengths and survival of age-0 fish. Since over-winter mortality (examined during a 1995-96 experiment) was found to be strongly size-selective, it follows that mechanisms acting in the first few weeks after hatching can ultimately affect the number of fish recruited to the next spawning season.

title: Life history of the flagfin shiner, Pteronotropis signipinnis, from a Mississippi blackwater stream

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, The University of Southern Mississippi, Hattiesburg, MS 39406-5018

abstract_text: The life history of the flagfin shiner, Pteronotropis signipinnis, was described from a population occurring in a second-order blackwater stream in southeast Mississippi. Analysis of length frequency histograms indicated a life span of one to two years. Females were reproductive from April to mid-August. Sex ratio was not significantly different from a 1:1 ratio. Adult males were larger and more heavily pigmented near the abdomen than females. All females reached sexual maturity by 27 mm SL and produced multiple clutches of ova. Clutch size ranged from 12 to 101 ova and was significantly correlated with SL. Mean mature oocyte diameter was 0.88 mm (range 0.76 to 0.96).

title: Revisiting a "textbook example" of natural selection in the wild: a field test of threat display convergence in threespine sticklebacks

authors.affiliation: Biology, Clark University, Worcester, MA 01610, USA

abstract_text: Freshwater populations of threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) exhibit a tremendous amount of adaptive variation in a number of traits. One classic example is male nuptial colouration in populations from the Chehalis River drainage basin in Washington State. Males in these populations assume a jet-black nuptial colouration, rather than the red underside and blue-green dorsum that is typical of the species. A widely cited, yet poorly tested, hypothesis to account for the evolution of the black nuptial colouration in these populations is the threat display convergence hypothesis. The hypothesis contends that the black nuptial colouration evolved in response to competition for nesting territories with the co-distributed Olympic mudminnow (Novumbra hubbsi), which is also black, territorial for nest sites and breeds at the same time of year as stickleback. The hypothesis produces the prediction that mudminnows have a greater impact on the reproductive success of typical, red male sticklebacks than on that of black male sticklebacks. I tested this prediction by manipulating the presence/absence of mudminnows and the colour type of stickleback present in screened exclosures in several wetland areas (typical nesting habitat for both species). Also, I conducted several field surveys of nesting sticklebacks to determine (i) the frequency and outcome of interactions between nesting sticklebacks and mudminnows and (ii) the temporal development of black nuptial coloration.

title: A molecular phylogenetic analysis of the relationships among the iguanid lizard genus Liolaemus: testing alternative biogeographic hypotheses

authors.affiliation: Washington University, Campus Box 1137, St. Louis, MO 63130-4899 USA

abstract_text: Liolaemus is a large genus of lizards in the family Iguanidae with greater than 160 species distributed throughout the southern half of South America on either side of the Andes. Relationships among Liolaemus species remain unresolved. Approximately 1800 bases of aligned mitochondrial DNA sequence data were obtained from regions encoding the ND1, ND2, COI, and eight transfer RNA genes. abstract_text: The presence of predatory fish is thought to restrict successful breeding by many amphibians, including Ambystoma maculatum (the spotted salamander), to temporary ponds. abstract_text: Winter's freezing temperatures exert a major selective force on temperate frogs and toads.
